instruction.text:
You will hear an excerpt from a podcast dealing with the history of the LGBTQIA+ movement. The hosts are presenting different historic milestones, current developments and data from new surveys, several figures are mentioned.

First, read the text. Then listen to the audio file below and fill in the figures into the blanks. Name one figure each, using the exact wording used in the recording.
instruction.sound: You will hear an excerpt from a podcast dealing with the history of the LGBTQIA+ movement. The hosts are presenting different historic milestones, current developments and data from new surveys, several figures are mentioned. First, read the text. Then listen to the audio file below and fill in the figures into the blanks. Name one figure each, using the exact wording used in the recording.

atoms.a: <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Okay, so today we’re doing some queer history, but I wanna thread it through what Americans say in surveys right now—because the movement isn’t just “then,” it’s literally shaping what people feel safe admitting out loud.</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Yeah, and you’re bringing receipts, right? Like, actual data?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Always. You know I like weaving history with data—because it keeps us honest about where we are, not just what we wish the ending was.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Great! So, why not give our audience a taste?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>All right, listen up. I'll tell you a number and you guess what it is, ok? So … Gallup has this report where 7.6% of U.S. adults (a) identify as L G B T Q I A +, or (b) support same-sex marriage.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Wait—7.6% is… support for same-sex marriage?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Nope, that’s identity. Support is a different number—hold that thought. And Gallup didn’t just ask, like, your cousin’s group chat. This study is very interesting in itself. It’s based on more than 12,000 interviews. And one of its key findings is that more than one in five Gen Z adults identify as queer.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Okay, that’s real. But before we dive straight into the specific survey results, could you first give us an overview of the history? Where did the movement start?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Well … That's not so easy to say. In the public memory, the classic U.S. turning-point story people point to is 1969—Stonewall. Not the first act of resistance ever, but a historic event that gets remembered and organized around. Over the years it got turned into this neat origin myth, but the more important part is: it created momentum. People started organizing more openly, and the movement got a much bigger public footprint.And returning to today’s poll numbers, of course the greater visibility changed what people say about themselves. But also, the movement wasn’t only about bars and raids and Pride marches—it was also about fighting institutional stigma. Have you ever heard the “Lavender Scare”?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>No, what's that?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>It’s basically the Cold War-era sibling of the Red Scare—except instead of hunting “communists,” the government treated suspected gay and lesbian federal employees as a security threat. The logic was ugly: if you’re closeted, you’re “vulnerable to blackmail,” so they said you can’t be trusted. That led to investigations, interrogations, people getting outed, and a ton of careers getting nuked—often without any real evidence beyond rumors. And what sticks with me is how bureaucratic it all was: policies, clearance rules, paperwork… like discrimination with an official stamp. It is estimated that at least 7,000 people were laid off or resigned at that time, but perhaps it was 10,000 or even more.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Wow. And there was no public outcry?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>No, quite the opposite. It was quite socially acceptable. Like, for a long time, being gay was treated as something “wrong” medically. Then the big professional bodies reversed that—first in U.S. psychiatry, later in global public health.One milestone there is 1973, when the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from their main diagnostic manual. That’s one of those changes where you can feel how huge it is: it didn’t magically end discrimination, but it took away this “official” stamp of pathology. In contrast, The World Health Assembly took quite a while, until 1990, to stop classifying homosexuality as a mental disorder in the international disease classification system as well.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Wow, at the height of the AIDS pandemic?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Yes. So you can imagine that it was quite controversial at the time. The CDC issued a statement at the time. Quote: “From 1981 through 1990, 100,777 deaths among persons with AIDS were reported to CDC by local, state, and territorial health departments; almost one third (31,196) of these deaths were reported during 1990.” So it certainly wasn't the case that this success suddenly made everything easy.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>That kind of shift matters for everything: families, schools, employers, even whether a person thinks, “If I say this out loud, am I putting a target on my back?”</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Yes, of course. It was a huge deal for the community, naturally.</voice>
atoms.b:
Due to a new survey ((7.6 7,6 7_point_6 seven_point_six))% of U.S. adults who identify as LGBTQIA+, including one in ((five 5)) Gen Zers.
The survey is based on more than ((12,000 12000 12.000 12k)) interviews.
The Stonewall Inn Riots took place in ((1969)).
At least ((7,000 7000 7.000 7k)) federal employees lost their jobs in the “Lavender Scare”.
In the US, homosexuality has not been considered a disease since ((1973)), and internationally since ((1990)).
Almost one ((third 1/3)) of AIDS-related deaths between 1981 and 1990 were reported in 1990.
